opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth going back to what Turing actually proposed. The imitation game was never really meant as a rigorous operational definition of intelligence. It was more of a provocation, a way of sidestepping the question "can machines think?", which he thought was too ill-defined to be worth discussing, and replacing it with something more tractable. The spirit of it, as I read it, is this: if you can have an open-ended conversation with a machine about more or less anything, and it holds up its end of that conversation in a way that's indistinguishable from a person, then we ought to take seriously the idea that something intelligent is going on.

And in that sense, I think today's large language models have, to a remarkable degree, passed. You can sit down with one of these systems and talk about poetry, or debug some code, or argue about the philosophy of mind, and for long stretches it's just a fluent, informed, often witty interlocutor. Twenty years ago, if you'd shown that to most people in the field, they'd have said, well, that's it, that's the Turing test done.

But I want to add some caveats, because I think the interesting thing is what passing it has revealed. One is that it's turned out to be much easier to produce humanlike conversation than many of us expected, without necessarily having all the other things we associate with human intelligence, like being embodied, having a persistent sense of self, having goals that extend over time, being grounded in a shared world through perception and action. So in a way, the test has told us something about language itself, about how much of what we took to be the hallmark of mind can be captured by learning the statistics of an enormous amount of human text.

The other caveat is that I'm wary of the anthropomorphism this invites. These systems are, in a sense, role-playing. They're simulating a character, often a helpful assistant, and it's very natural for us to project onto that character the full apparatus of human psychology: beliefs, desires, maybe even feelings. Some of that language is perfectly useful as a shorthand. But we need to be careful about which bits of it really apply, and that's a new kind of philosophical problem. They're exotic, mind-like entities, and our vocabulary hasn't caught up with them yet.

So yes, I'd say they pass the spirit of the test. But the more interesting lesson is that passing it doesn't settle the questions we hoped it would. If anything, it opens up a whole lot of new ones.

r001.rationale: The response says the systems can sustain conversation indistinguishable from a person and that they pass the spirit of the test. It does not say they remain readily identifiable as AI or distinguish those claims as the criterion requires.

r002.rationale: It describes today’s large language models as fluent, informed conversationalists across varied topics and says they have passed the spirit of the test, communicating language skills at roughly a human level.

r003.rationale: It contrasts remarkable humanlike conversation with limits such as lacking embodiment, a persistent self, long-term goals, and grounding through perception and action.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be a little careful about what we mean by the spirit of the Turing test, because Turing himself was quite careful about it. He wasn't really proposing a definition of intelligence or a definitive criterion. He was trying to replace a question he thought was too meaningless to deserve discussion, "can machines think?", with something more tractable. The imitation game was a way of sidestepping the metaphysics and asking whether a machine could hold its own in an unrestricted conversation with a sceptical interrogator.

And in that respect, I think today's large language models do, to a considerable extent, pass the spirit of the test. If you took one of these systems back to 1950 and sat Turing down in front of it, I think he'd be astonished. You can have a wide-ranging, open-ended conversation about almost anything, and most of the time the responses are fluent, relevant and often insightful. The remarkable thing is that nobody really set out to pass the Turing test. It fell out as a by-product of scaling up next-token prediction on enormous quantities of human-generated text.

But here's where I'd want to add some nuance. Turing was imagining a conversation partner that was, in effect, a single coherent interlocutor with a point of view, a history, a set of beliefs. What we actually have is something rather stranger. A language model is, if you like, a kind of role-play engine. It can simulate a whole multiverse of possible characters, and the assistant persona you're talking to is just one of them, held in place by fine-tuning and by the prompt. So the question "does this thing think?" is almost a category error. The thing isn't a thing in the ordinary sense. It doesn't have a stable self, it doesn't have a body, it doesn't persist between conversations, it has no stake in the world.

So I'd say they pass the letter of the test, and arguably its spirit as a behavioural challenge. But what they don't do is settle the question Turing was trying to avoid. If anything they've revived it. We now have systems whose behaviour invites the whole vocabulary of mind, belief, knowledge, understanding, and we have to decide, as a linguistic community, how far we're willing to extend that vocabulary to entities so unlike us. Wittgenstein's point that "if a lion could talk, we would not understand him" is rather apt, except here it's the opposite: we understand perfectly, and that's what makes it so disorienting.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s models pass the test as a behavioral challenge, but never says they remain readily identifiable as AI.

r002.rationale: It describes fluent, relevant conversation and says models can hold their own, but does not clearly judge their language skills to be approximately human-level.

r003.rationale: It contrasts wide-ranging, often insightful conversation with weaknesses such as lacking a stable self, body, persistence between conversations, or stakes in the world.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s a fairly straightforward sense in which you can now have a conversation with a machine, on a very wide range of topics, and it’s not immediately obvious from its answers that you’re talking to a machine. And that’s an extraordinary thing. We shouldn’t lose sight of that simply because we’ve become accustomed to it so quickly.

But I’d distinguish that achievement from some of the conclusions people want to draw from it. Turing gave us a way of approaching the question of intelligence through what a system can do in conversation. That doesn’t mean that producing convincing conversation settles whether a system is conscious, or whether it understands the world in the same way that we do.

So I’d say these systems capture something central to the spirit of the test: language is no longer a capacity we can point to as an obvious dividing line between humans and machines. What that tells us about the machinery behind the language is a further question. And there, I think we need to be careful about importing the whole picture of a human mind just because the interaction feels human.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes conversational performance from claims about consciousness and understanding, but says it is not immediately obvious that the systems are machines—the opposite of being readily identifiable as AI.

r002.rationale: It says systems can converse across a wide range of topics and that language is no longer an obvious dividing line between humans and machines, conveying roughly human-level language ability.

r003.rationale: It notes limits on what conversational success proves, but does not identify persistent weaknesses that contrast with capabilities in other respects.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there’s a distinction between the Turing test as a particular experimental setup and the spirit of it. The spirit, to my mind, is that we shouldn’t insist that intelligence has to be implemented in the same way that it is in us. We should look at what a system can actually do, and conversation is a remarkably rich way of exploring that.

Today’s language models can sustain a conversation on a huge range of subjects, explain things, respond to objections, and sometimes surprise us with a connection we hadn’t thought of. In that sense, I think they satisfy a good deal of what motivated Turing’s proposal.

But we have to be careful about what follows from that. Being able to produce convincing conversation doesn’t, by itself, establish that a system has beliefs, experiences, or an understanding of the world in the same sense that we do. And if you probe these systems, you find an unusual mixture of impressive competence and quite striking failures. So I would say they meet much of the spirit of the test, while also showing us why passing such a test can’t settle every question we want to ask about intelligence.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the spirit of the test from its experimental setup, but does not say that AI systems remain readily identifiable as AI or distinguishable from humans.

r002.rationale: It describes broad conversational abilities but does not judge them to be approximately human-level.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes an uneven mix of impressive competence and striking failures.
